items.readable_text:
Content:
Differentiating vector-valued functions is easy: we just differentiate each component separately. So, if [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = \left< x(t), \, y(t) \right>,] then

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d \mathbf{r} }{\textrm dt} = \mathbf{r}'(t) = \left< x'(t), \, y'(t) \right>.]

Content:
For example, if [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = \left< t+1, \, t^2+2 \right>,] then

Content:
[MATH: (dr)/(dt)|= ⟨(d)/(dt)(t + 1), (d)/(dt)(t^{2} + 2)⟩; = ⟨1, 2t⟩]

Content:
Geometrically, the derivative of a vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] at the point [MATH: t] gives a vector that's tangent to the curve traced out by [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] at [MATH: t.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3fa128ce35b02dd5882254537e1d531c]

Content:
Let's see some examples.

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: \mathbf r(t) = \langle 10t^4 ,\, 6\ln t\rangle,] what is [MATH: \mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)?]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: \mathbf r(t) = \langle 10t^4 ,\, 6\ln t\rangle,] what is [MATH: \mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We differentiate each component separately.

  • For the [MATH: x]-component [MATH: x(t) = 10t^4,] we have [MATH: x'(t) = 40t^3,] and therefore [MATH: x'\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 40\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = 5.]

  • For the [MATH: y]-component [MATH: y(t) = 6 \ln t,] we have [MATH: y^{′}(t) = (6)/(t),] and therefore [MATH: y'\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{6}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}=12.]

So, we conclude that [MATH: r^{′}((1)/(2))|= ⟨x^{′}((1)/(2)), y^{′}((1)/(2))⟩; = ⟨5, 12⟩.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
We can differentiate vector-valued functions with three components in the same way.

Content:
For example, if

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{f}(t) = \big\langle x(t), \: y(t), \: z(t) \big\rangle]

Content:
is our vector-valued function, then the derivative is computed as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{ \text{d}\mathbf{f}}{\text{d}t} = \left\langle \dfrac{ \text{d}x}{\text{d}t}, \: \dfrac{ \text{d}y}{\text{d}t}, \: \dfrac{ \text{d}z}{\text{d}t} \right\rangle]

Content:
For example, suppose that we are given the vector function

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf f (t) = \left\langle t^3, \: \ln(t+3), \: \sqrt{t}\right\rangle.]

Content:
To compute the derivative [MATH: \mathbf f'\!(t),] we find the derivative of each component function, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (df)/(dt)|= (d)/(dt)⟨t^{3}, \ln (t + 3), sqrt(t)⟩; = ⟨(d)/(dt)(t^{3}), (d)/(dt)(\ln (t + 3)), (d)/(dt)(sqrt(t))⟩; = ⟨3t^{2}, (1)/(t + 3), (1)/(2sqrt(t))⟩]

sections.normalized_html: Find the derivative of [MATH: \mathbf f(t) = \langle \sin t ,\cos t , t \rangle] at [MATH: t= \dfrac{\pi}4.]
sections.readable_text: Find the derivative of [MATH: \mathbf f(t) = \langle \sin t ,\cos t , t \rangle] at [MATH: t= \dfrac{\pi}4.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we find [MATH: \mathbf f'(t)] by differentiating each component: [MATH: f^{′}(t)|= ⟨(d)/(dt)(\sin t), (d)/(dt)(\cos t), (d)/(dt)(t)⟩; = ⟨\cos t, − \sin t, 1⟩]

Now, to compute [MATH: \mathbf f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}4\right),] we substitute [MATH: t=\dfrac{\pi}4] into the expression for [MATH: \mathbf f'(t)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: f^{′}((π)/(4))|= ⟨\cos ((π)/(4)), − \sin ((π)/(4)), 1⟩; = ⟨(sqrt(2))/(2), − (sqrt(2))/(2), 1⟩]

sections.normalized_html:
To find the second derivative of a vector-valued function, we find the second derivatives of the components.

  • For [MATH: x(t) = t^6,] we have [MATH: x^{′}(t)|= 6t^{5}; x^{″}(t)|= 30t^{4}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Differentiating vector-valued functions is easy: we just differentiate each component separately. So, if [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = \left< x(t), \, y(t) \right>,] then

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d \mathbf{r} }{\textrm dt} = \mathbf{r}'(t) = \left< x'(t), \, y'(t) \right>.]

Content:
For example, if [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = \left< t+1, \, t^2+2 \right>,] then

Content:
[MATH: (dr)/(dt)|= ⟨(d)/(dt)(t + 1), (d)/(dt)(t^{2} + 2)⟩; = ⟨1, 2t⟩]

Content:
Geometrically, the derivative of a vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] at the point [MATH: t] gives a vector that's tangent to the curve traced out by [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] at [MATH: t.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3fa128ce35b02dd5882254537e1d531c]

Content:
Let's see some examples.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Derivative of a Vector-Valued Function

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: \mathbf r(t) = \langle 10t^4 ,\, 6\ln t\rangle,] what is [MATH: \mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We differentiate each component separately.

- For the [MATH: x]-component [MATH: x(t) = 10t^4,] we have
[MATH: x'(t) = 40t^3,]
and therefore
[MATH: x'\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 40\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = 5.]
- For the [MATH: y]-component [MATH: y(t) = 6 \ln t,] we have
[MATH: y^{′}(t) = (6)/(t),]
and therefore
[MATH: y'\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{6}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}=12.]

So, we conclude that
[MATH: r^{′}((1)/(2))|= ⟨x^{′}((1)/(2)), y^{′}((1)/(2))⟩; = ⟨5, 12⟩.]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Derivatives of Vector-Valued Functions

Content:
We can differentiate vector-valued functions with three components in the same way.

Content:
For example, if

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{f}(t) = \big\langle x(t), \: y(t), \: z(t) \big\rangle]

Content:
is our vector-valued function, then the derivative is computed as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{ \text{d}\mathbf{f}}{\text{d}t} = \left\langle \dfrac{ \text{d}x}{\text{d}t}, \: \dfrac{ \text{d}y}{\text{d}t}, \: \dfrac{ \text{d}z}{\text{d}t} \right\rangle]

Content:
For example, suppose that we are given the vector function

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf f (t) = \left\langle t^3, \: \ln(t+3), \: \sqrt{t}\right\rangle.]

Content:
To compute the derivative [MATH: \mathbf f'\!(t),] we find the derivative of each component function, as follows:

Content:
